Items.Authors: Nuwanthika Fernando, Brent Miszalski, Nuria Lorente, Anthony Horton
Items.Title: MAVIS- Final design of the data reduction pipeline
Items.Abstract: MAVIS is the MCAO Assisted Visible Imager and Spectrograph, the first MCAO-facility instrument planned for the VLT which will provide a near diffraction-limited view of the visible wavelength. We present the final design for the Data Reduction Pipeline of the instrument, and describe the prototyping for the design of calibration methods and dataflows. For the spectrograph calibrations, the geometry of the slices is determined using a series of moving pinhole mask exposures. Prototyping the geometry recipe resulted in the change to the pinhole mask design. This also confirmed the need for etalons for the wavelength calibration, to achieve required accuracies in the low resolution blue mode. Early prototyping of the DRS has been beneficial to the design of the entire instrument. The critical algorithms used ESO’s PyCPL libraries, the GNU Scientific Library, and data workflows at each stage were drafted using the new EDPS (ESO Data Processing System) libraries.

Items.Authors: S. Perez, M. Bonati, B. Cervantes, A. Lapi, A. Varela, E. Schiller, A. Drlica-Wagner, G. Damke, C. Chavez, J. Estrada, G. Pinaroli, G. Fernandez-Moroni, M. Makler, J. Tiffenberg
Items.Title: SkipperCam: a wide-field skipper-CCD pathfinder for high-cadence imaging with sub-electron capabilities
Items.Abstract: We present SkipperCam, a Skipper-CCD imager pathfinder demonstrating low-noise, high-cadence wide-field imaging. It deploys a 20-sensor Skipper-CCD focal plane (~27 Mpix) on the 0.6 m Curtis–Schmidt telescope at CTIO, reusing the PreCam camera body, shutter, and filter wheel. A massively parallel, MIDNA-based readout decouples the usual trade-off between low noise and slow readout, delivering a ~2 deg² field of view with ~2 s full-frame cadence and ~7 e⁻ noise in fast survey mode, while reaching sub-electron noise via multiple non-destructive sampling. Primarily a technology demonstrator, it is also optimized for early science through a high-cadence microlensing survey of the Large Magellanic Cloud targeting short-timescale events from low-mass compact objects, with opportunities in photometric variability, transient detection, blue-sensitive imaging, and stellar-occultation follow-ups. SkipperCam is the first on-sky demonstration of a multiplexed Skipper-CCD array in survey mode.

Items.Authors: Takumi Hagiwara, Taku Nakayama, Subaru Shibai, Shoki Iwaguchi, Yutaro Enomoto, Kiwamu Izumi
Items.Title: Telescope of lossless intersatellite laser ranging for the SILVIA formation flying mission
Items.Abstract: This work proposes an optical telescope architecture for intersatellite laser interferometry missions SILVIA, where lossless intersatellite laser ranging is employed.    To simplify link acquisition and reduce reliance on satellite attitude control, we propose a non-cooperative laser link approach. However, this approach poses two major challenges: both retroreflection and mode matching must be simultaneously achieved, and sharing a single telescope for transmission and reception makes independent bidirectional alignment nontrivial.    To overcome these issues, we propose a new telescope design inspired by the cat’s-eye retroreflector and derive its parameters using ray-matrix analysis. Based on this design, we are currently developing an optical breadboard model (BBM). This talk presents the design concept and reports on the current BBM development status.

Items.Authors: Boudewijn Hut, Carla J. Baldovin Saveedra, Cees Bassa, Ilse van Bemmel, André Gunst, Tom Kamphuis, Ronald Roelfsema, John Swinbank, Sander ter Veen
Items.Title: Towards the LOFAR2.0 Observatory: Our Engineering Journey
Items.Abstract: The world's largest low-frequency (10-240MHz) radio telescope is undergoing a major upgrade of its hardware, firmware and software to improve its unique observing capabilities. A variety of scientific use cases, ranging from galaxy evolution, transients and cosmic rays to space weather and lightning research is targeted. This pan-European Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) is continuously improved by ASTRON and its partners to keep it a world class telescope.     Given the science goals of the LOFAR2.0 upgrade, we present an overview of the main design challenges and key solutions by our multi-disciplinary team: from antenna, mechanical, network and software to systems engineering and high-performance computing. We also present our approach to integrate the solutions into the new LOFAR2.0 Observatory.

Items.Authors: Parker T. Johnson, Jared R. Males, Povilas Palunas, Olivier Guyon, Sebastiaan Haffert, Joseph Long, Vincent Deo, Julien Lozi, Laird Close, Maggie Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Jialin Li, Joshua Liberman, Miles Lucas, Matthijs Mars, Eden McEwen, Tiffany Nguyen, Elena Tonucci, Katie Twitchell
Items.Title: Sensor fusion on MagAO-X: real time vibration control using accelerometers
Items.Abstract: Mechanical vibrations are a major source of residual wavefront error (WFE) in adaptive optics (AO) systems and can limit high-contrast imaging performance. We present a low-cost, modular accelerometer telemetry system on the MagAO-X extreme AO instrument at the 6.5 m Clay Magellan Telescope. The system uses accelerometers and a Raspberry Pi based acquisition to stream synchronized telemetry to the real-time control computer with microsecond-level timing stability. Accelerometer measurements identified dominant vibration sources, including the primary mirror glycol pump and the secondary mirror actuation and autofocus systems. Coherence analysis shows that approximately one-third of the residual tip and tilt WFE is correlated with structural vibrations. An empirical orthogonal function predictor achieved offline variance reductions of 23% in tip and 37% in tilt. These results demonstrate the potential of accelerometer telemetry for vibration identification and predictive AO control.

Items.Authors: Locke D. Spencer, Christopher Benson, Thomas Essenger-Hileman, William Grainger, David Leisawitz, Lee Mundy, Ettore Pedretti, Berke V. Ricketti, Giorgio Savini, Jeremy P. Scott, Gerard van Belle, David Wilner
Items.Title: Technology development for space-based far-infrared double Fourier interferometry
Items.Abstract: Many fundamental questions leading astrophysics research require observations with high resolution spectroscopy and imaging at high spatial resolution, i.e., hyper-spectral imaging, in the Far-Infrared (Far-IR). Topics include: the origin of the universe, conditions for star and planet formation, and, ultimately, the conditions for the emergence of life. Over half of the energy emitted by the Universe appears in the relatively unexplored Far-IR spectral region, most of which is opaque from ground-based sites necessitating space-borne instrumentation.   We discuss the motivating science and technology development supporting Far-IR Double Fourier Interferometry instrumentation, requisite components, and associated technology requisite for the advancement of a Far-IR Double Fourier Interferometry space mission. This includes development of digital simulation tools, laboratory instrumentation development and demonstration, and exploration of the science potential of such a facility.

Items.Authors: Emily M. Witt, Brian T. Fleming, Stephan McCandliss, Isu Ravi, Vida Saeedzadeh, Jason Tumlinson, Sarah Tuttle, Cassandra Lochhaas, Matilde Mingozzi, Briana Indahl, Manuel Quijada
Items.Title: The Juniper CubeSat: mission operations
Items.Abstract: The circumgalactic media (CGM) of galaxies play a key role in the baryon cycle of galactic feedback. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the CGM in particular is crucial to understanding the flow of gas and metals into and out of galaxies. To characterize this process, the Juniper 16U CubeSat mission has been designed to conduct observations of the CGM of nearby galaxies in multiple far ultraviolet (FUV) bandpasses that include key metal lines such as O VI (103.5 nm), C II (133.5 nm), and C IV (154.9 nm). Juniper will observe the CGM of roughly ten galaxies and will conduct weekly calibration observations to characterize the performance of the new FUV technologies that enable Juniper's unprecedented spectral resolution. This proceedings will overview the current mission status and discuss the planned mission operations for Juniper.

Items.Authors: Samantha Walker, Austin Kaczmarek, Douglas Bennett, Darshan Patel, Jason Austermann, Shannon Duff, Johannes Hubmayr, Kelsey Morgan, Dan Schmidt, Daniel Swetz, Joel Ullom, Anna Vaskuri, Michael Vissers, Joel Weber, Jordan Wheeler, Michael Niemack, Katja Nowack
Items.Title: Visualizing the properties of astronomical superconducting detectors with scanning SQUID microscopy
Items.Abstract: Large arrays of superconducting detectors, such as transition-edge sensors (TESs) and kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs), are being used in an increasing number of experiments across the electromagnetic spectrum. However, there remain gaps in our understanding of detector physics. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy (SSM), we directly visualize (sub)millimeter and X-ray TESs and KIDs with micrometer-scale spatial resolution at sub-Kelvin temperatures. For TESs, we image a direct superconducting proximity effect, where the TES acts as a weak link between superconducting leads, and an inverse proximity effect with normal metal structures. We visualize the current distribution in voltage-biased TESs. For KIDs, we directly image vortex configurations in different regions of the device. Our work has implications for understanding how design choices affect TES and KID operation and aims to lead to more optimal arrays for future observatories.

Items.Authors: Guido Cupani, Valentina D'Odorico, Stefano Cristiani, Simona Di Stefano, Christian Piscitelli, Andrea Trost
Items.Title: Astrocook v2: LLM-Ready Foundation for Autonomous Analysis of Quasar Spectra
Items.Abstract: Astrocook v2 represents a major architectural redesign of the well-known quasar analysis tool. It is built on an immutable data core, a decoupled API, and a new PySide6 GUI. This system guarantees stability, high performance, and readiness for external integration.    We highlight the successful implementation of a robust SciPy-based Voigt Fitter and a powerful Parameter Constraints workflow. This system enables full parameter linking (Value/Thermal modes) and dynamic evaluation. The core strength is reproducible, controlled analysis, supported by the SystemListV2 as the Single Source of Truth for component grouping and the interactive System Inspector for efficient component manipulation.    This stable foundation, with its immutable API and fully constrained physical model, is engineered for integration with Large Language Models (LLMs). Astrocook will leverage AI reasoning for guiding complex analysis sequences, advancing toward autonomous pipelines for future spectroscopic surveys.

Items.Authors: Laurane Fréour, Anna Puglisi, Amelia Bayo, Fatemeh Zahra Majidi, Sabine Thater, Francesca Primas, Laurence Tresse, Umberto Rescigno, Maria Cristina Fortuna, Stéphanie Escoffier, Letizia P. Cassarà, Roland Bacon, Vincenzo Mainieri, Sofia Randich
Items.Title: Embedding Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion in the WST collaboration
Items.Abstract: The proposed Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a next-generation telescope facility with a 12-meter primary mirror that may be operational in the 2040s. The project has a broad range of scientific goals and engages a large Community of more than 1000 members across multiple time zones, institutions, career stages, and professional roles. As for any large-scale scientific collaboration, building WST is therefore not only a technical and scientific challenge, but also a social and organisational one. This is particularly important in Astronomy and STEM disciplines more broadly, where marginalized groups remain underrepresented, particularly in leadership positions.     In this paper, we describe the creation and first year of activity of the WST Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) working group. We discuss how the group has worked to embed EDI considerations into the early phases of the Collaboration, and we present our ongoing and future projects.

Items.Authors: Giuseppe Sottile, Pierluca Sangiorgi, Fabio Lo Gerfo, Carmelo Gargano, Mattia Corpora, Davide Mollica, Giovanni Contino, Teresa Mineo, Giovanni Pareschi, Michele Buzzi, Salvatore Scuderi, Antonio Miccichè, Giuseppe Leto, Gaetano Nicotra, Eugenio Martinetti, Giancarlo Bellassai, Michele Bellassai, Carmelo Lauretta, Salvatore Garozzo, Davide Marano, Andrea Abba, Francesco Caponio, Alberto Cusimano, Julien Fleury, Florent Perez, Salleh Ahmad, Jean Baptiste Cizel, Gino Tosti, Alberto Segreto
Items.Title: First results from the ASTRI Mini-Array air-Cherenkov cameras
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array, led by INAF, will deploy nine dual-mirror air-Cherenkov telescopes at the Teide Observatory (Tenerife), using the Schwarzschild–Couder configuration. Seven telescopes are installed, with two already acquiring Cherenkov data during commissioning and science verification. The ASTRI camera features a 10.5° Field of View and 2,368 SiPM pixels read out by the CITIROC ASIC, enabling fast, low-power signal extraction. These features guided the design of a compact and robust Peltier-based focal-plane thermal-control system, which eliminates the need for external liquid cooling, while the SiPM bias system provides the high currents needed for high-duty-cycle observations under elevated Night Sky Background conditions. The Back-End Electronics manages all operations and achieves sub-nanosecond synchronization via the White Rabbit system. Initial results confirm that the ASTRI camera design meets the scientific and operational requirements for full array deployment.

Items.Authors: Ruslan Belikov, Dan Sirbu, Eduardo Bendek, David Marx, Camilo Mejia Prada, Hanying Zhou, Byong-Joon Seo, Jonathan W. Lin, Kevin F. Sims
Items.Title: Multi-star wavefront control: updates on science opportunities for Roman CGI and HWO, and latest progress in technology development
Items.Abstract: This work presents the latest technology development and science opportunities for Multi-Star Wavefront Control (MSWC), a method to enable high-contrast imaging of multi-star systems with the Roman Space Telescope and Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). MSWC enhances the exoplanet yield and enables new science specific to planets around multi-star systems. In addition, it enables a follow up of the aCenA planet candidate recently reported by JWST. Our laboratory tests are continuing at JPL’s High Contrast Imaging Testbed (HCIT), and at time of this writing, include a demonstration of 9.4e-8 in full MSWC mode for an equivalent aCenAB separation. Scaled to the binary’s actual flux ratio, these performance levels yield equivalent contrasts of 3.7e-8 (aCenA) and 1.8e-7 (aCenB). These results suggest that current performance may already be sufficient to detect planets around aCenA in reflected light, if it can be replicated on sky.

Items.Authors: Satoki Matsushita, Keiichi Asada, Chih-Wei Huang, Cristina Romero-Canizales, Nimesh Patel, Jongho Park, Britton Jeter, Minchul Kam, Rema J. Ahmid, Pierre Martin-Cocher, Cheng-Yu Kuo, Jun Yi Koay, Ming-Tang Chen, Chih-Chiang Han, Derek Kubo, Yu-Chieh Huang, Philippe Raffin, Shu-Hao Chang, Ta-Shun Wei, Jia-Ruei Nian, Pai-An Chen, Peter Oshiro, Sally Lau, Timothy Norton, Tirupati K. Sridharan, Ramprasad Rao, Jacob Hawthorne, Keara Carter, Sheperd Doeleman, Jose Soto, Hannah Rana, Thomas R. Greve, Paul Ho
Items.Title: Science operation and status updates of the Greenland Telescope (GLT)
Items.Abstract: Primary scientific goal of the Greenland Telescope (GLT) project is to image black hole shadows using (sub)millimeter-wave Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique together with other (sub)millimeter telescopes around the world. It has a 12-m diameter dish, and operating at frequencies of 86, 230, and 345 GHz. It is currently located at the Pituffik Space Base (former Thule Air Base), and is regularly joining VLBI observations, such as Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and Global Millimeter VLBI Array (GMVA). In parallel, we accumulated data on pointing, aperture efficiency measurements, etc., at all three frequencies. We recently upgraded the receiver optics, and confirmed that all the receivers have almost the same focus positions and the pointings, which is the first step for the simultaneous multi-frequency operation. We also performed photogrammetry and holography to improve the surface accuracy. Here, we will report the latest activities and telescope characteristics.

Items.Authors: Zhenyuan Sun, Stafford Withington, Songyuan Zhao, Wei Chen
Items.Title: Analysis of resonance circular distortions in superconducting resonators against two dissipative nonlinear models at low and high readout power regimes
Items.Abstract: Experimental measurements of superconducting microwave resonators reveal distinct distortions of the resonance circle in the complex plane: a ‘teardrop’ shape at low readout power and a ‘squashed’ shape at high power. We compare these observations with two representative dissipative models—the two-level system (TLS) model at low power and quasiparticle heating (QPH) at high power. Both models show reasonable agreement with the measured distortions: TLS accurately reproduces the low-power teardrop, while QPH closely matches the high-power squashed morphology. Although other mechanisms may contribute in general at high power ranges, they are not necessary to explain the data presented here. These results demonstrate that resonance-circle morphology, when combined with dissipative models, serves as a practical diagnostic tool for identifying dominant loss behaviour in superconducting resonators for cryogenic detector and readout applications.

Items.Authors: Yuri Evangelista, Francesco Ceraudo, Giovanni Della Casa, Ettore Del Monte, Giuseppe Dilillo, Marco Feroci, Edoardo Giancarli, Alessio Nuti, Riccardo Campana, Mauro Fiorini, Giovanni Lombardi, Massimo Rapisarda, Ajay Sharma, Giuseppe Bertuccio, Filippo Mele, Yinhe Zhu, Marco Grassi, Piero Malcovati, Jacopo Giani, Marco Tambussi, Matias Antonelli, Alexandre Rachevski, Irina Rashevskaya, Gianluigi Zampa, Nicola Zampa, Evgeny Demenev, Giancarlo Pepponi, Francesco Ficorella, Nicola Zorzi, Francesca Esposito, Immacolata Donnarumma, Alessandro Turchi, Ugo Cortesi, Fabio D'Amico, Marco Gai, Andrea Argan
Items.Title: LEM-X: an all sky monitor for the Moon's surface
Items.Abstract: LEM-X is an all-sky X-ray observatory proposed for the surface of the Moon. Its primary scientific goal is to enhance multi-messenger astrophysics by detecting and monitoring high-energy transient phenomena and variable X-ray sources across the sky.  The building block of LEM-X is a pair of coded aperture cameras, able to image the sky in a field of view of 2sr (FWZR) with a source location accuracy of 1 arcmin. The LEM-X instrument envisages multiple camera pairs in a dome-shaped structure, with each camera designed to achieve a sensitivity better than 5 mCrab in 50ks and 1 Crab in 1s in a wide energy band (2-50 keV).  The sensitive elements of LEM-X are large area linear Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) read-out by custom low-noise ASICs, which provide excellent spectral-timing performance. The energy resolution at room temperature is better than 350 eV FWHM at 6 keV, with 10 us time resolution.  In this contribution we describe the LEM-X design and report about its development status.

Items.Authors: Mrunmayi S. Deshpande, Nuria P. F. Lorente, Tony Farrell, Satyam Mishra
Items.Title: Modernising Observatory Control: Integrating Legacy DRAMA with Next-Generation Instrumentation
Items.Abstract: The DRAMA (Distributed Real-Time AAO Monitor for Astronomy) framework was first developed at Anglo-Australian Observatory (AAO) in the early 1990s, Designed in C, C++, DRAMA provides a distributed, message-based control architecture. This robust design powers some of the most important astronomical instruments assembled at AAO — from the robot fibre positioner 2dF, spectrographs such as AAOmega, HERMES. DRAMA’s reliability and modular, task-oriented, real-time behaviour have also attracted international adoption. As new instruments are being developed at the AAO we are updating the DRAMA environment to meet modern software engineering and deployment practices. Recent efforts include containerising DRAMA using Docker and creating a modern Python interface. Currently, DRAMA continues to play an active role: it is used in the newly built KSPEC spectrograph for the KMTNet telescope, and forms the control architecture for the high-resolution spectrograph for the Devasthal Optical Telescope

Items.Authors: Ashley D. Baker, Nemanja Jovanovic, Dimitri Mawet, William Melby, Andrew Howard, Jake Zimmer, Samuel Halverson
Items.Title: System testing and characterization of HIRAX, an ultra-narrow multi-band imager for transit spectroscopy of hot Jupiters
Items.Abstract: HIRAX is a multi-band imager for the Hale telescope using ultra-narrow bandpasses centered around the sodium doublet in order to perform transit spectroscopy of hot Jupiters. It uses three 4Å wide bandpass filters each cascaded at an angle to utilize the out-of-band reflection to image a star simultaneously in the three bands, which provides a self-reference to reduce systematic effects. The goal of HIRAX is to understand the merits and limitations with this instrument architecture. To study this, HIRAX will be tested on sky in summer of 2026 with the Hale telescope by observing well-studied hot Jupiter planets with past sodium observations. Here we present commissioning activities done for HIRAX in prep for on-sky observations of HD189733b. These activities include setting up its new filter thermal control system, testing the spectral stability of the narrowband filter bandpasses, and measuring the photometric stability in lab.

Items.Authors: Solvay A. Blomquist, Hyukmo Kang, Maggie Kautz, Simran Agarwal, Kelsey Miller, Kyle Van Gorkom, Corey Fucetola, Heejoo Choi, Patrick Ingraham, Ewan S. Douglas, Daewook Kim, Sanchit Sabhlok, Alexandra Kupersmith, Adam Schilperoort
Items.Title: Tiny Observatory for Telescope Optimization (TOTO): testing algorithms for autonomous on-orbit alignment for space-based telescope systems
Items.Abstract: The Tiny Observatory for Telescope Optimization (TOTO) is an optical testbed designed to evaluate the efficacy of autonomously driven alignment algorithms for space-based telescope systems. For space-based missions, active control of the telescope on-orbit offers potential to relax passive alignment requirements and reduce on-ground verification activity. TOTO is used to evaluate and verify simulation work of two primary alignment algorithms, Stochastic Parallel Gradient Descent (SPGD) and focus-diverse phase retrieval. Previous simulation work has confirmed that by using SPGD for coarse alignment followed by focus-diverse phase retrieval for fine alignment, we can reach diffraction-limited performance on-orbit. This paper presents the results of the autonomous alignment algorithm of a TMA using TOTO. We report the current status of TOTO as well as preliminary results from SPGD and phase retrieval on the testbed using monochromatic light source to simulate a natural guide star.

Items.Authors: Lun-Jun Liu, Reinier Janssen, Jonathon Hunacek, Talia Saeid, Justin Bracks, Steve Hailey-Dunsheath, Shubh Agrawal, Charles Bradford, James Aguirre, Hrushi Athreya, Brockton Brendal, Bruce Bumble, Jeffrey Filippini, Jianyang Fu, Karolina Garcia, Christopher Groppi, Dylan Joralmon, Wooseok Kang, Garrett Keating, Ryan Keenan, Ian Lowe, Alex Manduca, Daniel Marrone, Philip Mauskopf, Evan Mayer, Sydnee O'Donnell, Simon Tartakovsky, Mathilde Van Cuyck, Joaquin Vieira, Jessica Zebrowski
Items.Title: Characterization of the laser-trimmed 317-420 μm KID array for the Terahertz Intensity Mapper
Items.Abstract: We present improved performance of the kinetic inductance detector (KID) array for the Terahertz Intensity Mapper (TIM). TIM is NASA-funded balloon mission aimed at probing the peak of cosmic star formation. The TIM payload is equipped with two spectral bands, 240–420 μm and 317–420 μm, each employing a focal plane of four-kilopixel wafers of lumped-element KIDs. Previous characterization of the 317–420 μm arrays revealed resonator collisions in the readout band, limiting the number of usable detectors and motivating optimization of resonator frequency spacing. To increase the number of science usable KIDs, here we present a strategy to redistribute resonator frequencies and apply laser trimming to shorten a small length of the resonator’s interdigitated capacitor. Measurements of the trimmed array show substantial improvement in frequency spacing and in the fraction of resonators meeting science requirements. In addition, we discuss planned refinements for subsequent TIM KID arrays.

Items.Authors: Branden Allen
Items.Title: Initial detector characterization and performance for the Portable Lunar Observer for Volatiles, Environment, and Resources (PLOVER)
Items.Abstract: The Portable Lunar Observer for Volatiles, Environment, and Resources (PLOVER) was conceived as a multi-use instrument package consisting of three instruments: (1) the Wide-band Internal Neutron and Gamma-ray Spectrometer (WINGS) a large-volume CLYC-based scintillator detector which is simultaneously sensitive to, and capable of detecting and discriminating between incident X/γ-rays and neutrons; (2) The Advanced Visible Infrared Analytic Spectrometer (AVIANS) a VIS/IR hyperspectral imager for simultaneous interrogation of surface mineralogy, and (3) CZT Advanced Imager for the Lunar Surface (TAILS) a high-resolution Compton imager to resolve nearby anomalies in the composition of the lunar surface.    Here we discuss the overall instrument design and deployment opportunities, expected performance and prospects, as well as the initial testing of the CLYC detectors in the laboratory and in the field at the summit of Maunakea.

Items.Authors: Jaime Ruíz-Díaz-Soto, Jorge Fuentes-Fernandez, Fernando Angeles, José Leonardo Garces, Alejandro Farah, Sebastian F. Sanchez
Items.Title: 3D printing in astronomy: mechanical design and optomechanical solutions using precision additive manufacturing in the EBANO instrument
Items.Abstract: The ÉBANO spectrograph stands out for its innovative design and fabrication using additive manufacturing (3D printing). Approximately 70% of its optomechanical components are manufactured from engineering polymers, meeting all scientific requirements. The mechanical design is based on flexible tolerances, which allowed the entire system to be manufactured using precision 3D printing. This approach significantly reduced cost, mass, and production time compared to traditional methods, while simplifying design adjustments and maintaining excellent optical performance. This work presents the design, manufacturing process, assembly, and verification of these components, demonstrating the feasibility of additive manufacturing for high-quality astronomical instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Jie Liu, Wei Wang, Jie Hu, Dong Liu, Jing Li, Shengcai Shi
Items.Title: A 0.3–5GHz low‑power cryogenic amplifier based on SiGe HBT technology for large‑scale detector arrays
Items.Abstract: We have developed low-power cryogenic low-noise amplifiers (LNAs) based on SiGe heterojunction bipolar transistor (HBT) technology. The amplifier consumes only 5 mW, making it well-suited for direct integration into next-generation large pixel count receivers without inducing significant thermal load on superconducting detectors. We extracted the small‑signal and noise model parameters of the HBT at 4 K. Based on this circuit model, we designed a 0.3-5 GHz cryogenic low-noise amplifier. Experimental results show that the amplifier achieves a typical gain of 37 dB and a noise temperature of approximately 6 K at an ambient temperature of 4 K. The combination of low power dissipation, low noise temperature, and wide bandwidth makes this amplifier particularly well- suited for use in large‑format microwave kinetic inductance detector (KID) arrays for Xue-shan-mu-chang Submillimeter Telescope (XSMT).

Items.Authors: Edoardo Borciani, Riccardo Campana, Fabio Muleri, Giuseppe Baldazzi, Claudio Labanti, Ezequiel J. Marchesini, Enrico Virgilli, Lorenzo Amati, Giulia Mattioli, Paolo Calabretto, Ajay Sharma, Alfonso Pisapia, Farangis Takdehghan, Sofia Cussini
Items.Title: A 3D Compton polarimeter for the SWIPE mission concept
Items.Abstract: We present the development of a prototype for SWIPE (Soft-X and -ray WIde-field polarimeter) mission concept, which integrates photoelectric (0.2–8 keV) and Compton (20–200 keV) polarimeters for transient astrophysics. The novel Compton polarimeter utilizes scintillator bars coupled to double-ended readout electronics (Si-PM/SDDs). This configuration allows the reconstruction of the Depth of Interaction (DOI). Direct DOI knowledge enables reconstructing the polar scattering angle, and thus of the full scattering kinematics, optimizing the minimum detectable polarization. We report experimental tests of this approach, including DOI performance, spatial and energy resolution.

Items.Authors: Guillermo Martin, Louis Gemmerlé, Manon Lallement, Myriam Bonduelle, Jean-Philippe Berger, Roland Salut, Laurent Robert, Nadège Courjal, Germain Garreau, Denis Defrère
Items.Title: A 4T mid IR, double Bracewell, beam combiner in lithium niobate for high contrast interferometry
Items.Abstract: A novel 4 telescope beam combiner photonic chip, using a Lithium Niobate based technological platform in the mid IR, has been developed. These chips are devoted for instruments such as ASGAARD-NOTT for VLTI [1] or future spatial projects such as LIFE [2]. The single mode targeted spectral region is the L’-Band (3.4 - 4.1um). The goal of this work is to study the performances of the photonic chip: transmission, polarization behavior and achromaticity within this band. In particular, we will focus on the coupling ratio obtained in the directional couplers, the rejection ratio achieved and its spectral bandwidth. This different results were obtained using a 2T nulling bench developed at IPAG [3], and the 4T nulling bench developed at KU Leuven [4]

Items.Authors: Ian P. McLean, Jeremy T. Lin, Pradip Gatkine
Items.Title: A compact high-performance imaging platform for NIR photonic instrumentation
Items.Abstract: This work presents a compact, thermally stabilized imaging platform designed for NIR photonic-chip integration and low-light astronomical or remote-sensing applications. The system uses staged thermoelectric coolers, heat pipes, and custom control electronics to maintain stable temperatures during long exposures. Stray light is reduced with broadband-absorbent materials, black-anodized surfaces, internal baffles, and low-reflection lens and filter holders. A light-sealed lens interface suppresses scattering from threaded elements, while vibration-damping structures improve mechanical stability. Custom acquisition software manages exposure settings, thermal states, and calibration steps, providing transparency into system behavior and enabling flexible spectral-analysis workflows. Initial tests show reduced thermal noise, suppressed internal reflections, and improved signal-to-noise ratios, demonstrating a strong foundation for future compact photonic instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Cristian Manzoni, Matteo Corti, Fabrizio Preda, Antonio Perri, Giulio Cerullo, Gianluca Valentini, Ondřej Ballada, Čestmír Barta, Matteo Mallia
Items.Title: A compact hyperspectral camera for remote sensing from the ultraviolet to the thermal infrared
Items.Abstract: We introduce a compact hyperspectral camera based on the time-domain Fourier-transform approach, equipped with an ultrastable birefringent interferometer. The time-domain approach enables hyperspectral imaging with shorter acquisition times and higher spectral accuracy compared to standard dispersive optics. We provide experimental proofs of the camera capability by performing remote-sensing measurements in the visible and near-infrared range. Recently we extended the spectral range to the thermal infrared, where vibrational transitions associated with chemical bonds have their absorption. Due to its compactness, lightweight and extreme stability even in harsh environments, the camera is a unique enabling technology for remote unambiguous chemical identification.

Items.Authors: Colin Cunningham, Carolyn Atkins, Beth Biller, Mark McCaughrean, Stephen Todd
Items.Title: A giant telescope manufactured in space?
Items.Abstract: We explore a concept for a giant telescope manufactured in space to enable a primary mirror of 100m diameter. This is combined with a module containing a secondary mirror, correction optics and a prime focus instrumentation, flying in formation at about 1000m from the primary mirror. We assume that deployment of such a large primary mirror in space would require that a large fraction of the system would need to be manufactured in space in order to minimise launch costs, although that trade-off may now be changing with potential advances in heavy-lift capabilities. The enormous challenges of such a project mean that it would be many decades before the technology is possible, but when it is we could have unprecedented angular resolution and sensitivity and consequent breakthroughs in many areas, with exoplanet characterisation being the stand out application. Potential technical solutions are presented, leading to discussion of the potential scientific capability.

Items.Authors: Louis H. Marting, Kenichi Karatsu, Leon G. G. Olde Scholtenhuis, Shahab O. Dabironezare, Arend Moerman, David J. Thoen, Ton J. van der Linden, Akira Endo, Jochem J. A. Baselmans
Items.Title: A high efficiency filterbank using directional filters for integral field spectrometers in the millimeter/sub-millimeter band
Items.Abstract: Superconducting on-chip spectrometers are advancing rapidly, and large imaging spectrometers are quickly becoming feasible in the sub-mm band. These imaging spectrometers are ideally equipped to advance our understanding of several exciting astronomical signals that describe the evolution of our Universe. This includes SZ effect observations, CMB polarimetry, LIM and tomography of terahertz line-emitting galaxies (TLEG). These science cases all require imaging spectrometers with moderate spectral resolution and a large bandwidth, however, the state-of-the-art sub-mm instruments have come short in reaching the required sensitivity.    In this contribution, we experimentally demonstrate a new type of filter for on-chip spectrometers, called a directional filter, with a measured filter efficiency of 75%. This filter improves upon the conventionally used half-wave filters, which typically have an efficiency of 25% or less. We aim to implement this design on the TIFUUN instrument.

Items.Authors: Homin Jiang, Bishnu K. Sharma
Items.Title: A high‑speed direct RF sampling FPGA platform for high-frequency radio telescope backends
Items.Abstract: High-speed ADCs operating at GSps rates enable the direct digitization of wideband RF signals, significantly reducing reliance on complex analog downconversion chains. This approach minimizes distortion and phase noise while extending spectral coverage. Recent advances, such as Altera’s integration of 8-bit ADCs capable of sampling at up to 64 GSps, support bandwidths exceeding 32 GHz and greatly simplify the IF section.  We present the development of a 64 GSps high-speed digitization system based on Altera’s Direct RF FPGA platform, utilizing the Stratix 10 AX FPGA evaluation kit. The platform incorporates 64 GSps ADC chiplets and an embedded Direct RF IP core. Preliminary testing with a 26.5 GHz wideband noise source and notch filter demonstrates promising performance in 64 GSps mode. This system represents a significant step toward next-generation digital backends and will be well-suited for high-frequency radio telescopes such as the JCMT and the GLT.

Items.Authors: Thomas M. Herbst, José R. Sánchez-Gallego, Armin Böhm, Lars Mohr
Items.Title: A low cost, thermal infrared, all-sky cloud camera
Items.Abstract: We describe the design, construction, and testing of a compact, thermal infrared, all-sky camera based on commercial radiometric modules from FLIR. Five wide-angle Lepton 3.1r cameras provide full sky coverage above 30° elevation with ~0.5° spatial resolution. A 6th camera would allow full, hemispheric imaging. The entire system requires only a single Power Over Ethernet connection and fits within a 20 cm weatherproof housing. Using 3D-printed components and a simple NUC-type linux computer, the total cost of the all-sky camera is approximately €1000.

Items.Authors: Christopher S. Benson, Peter S. Barry, Patrick Ashworth, Harry Gordon-Moys, Izaak Morris
Items.Title: A low-noise Fourier transform survey spectrometer leveraging on-chip spectrometers
Items.Abstract: The development of wide- field-of-view (FoV) medium-resolution (medium-R) mapping spectrometers has been identified as a priority in millimetre/sub-millimeter astronomy for future and existing facilities. Spectrometer architectures that have been historically used for this purpose have significant technical hurdles that limit their performance. To combat the inherent noise in Fourier Transform Spectrometers (FTSs) and achieve an effective R~2000 mapping spectrometer in the near term, we propose combining a medium-R FTS with a low-resolution on-chip Filterbank Spectrometer (FBS) focal plane as a post-dispersion mechanism. In this arrangement, an FBS with only a modest resolution is sufficient to dramatically improve sensitivity without compromising the fundamental imaging advantages of the FTS. We present our progress in the laboratory validation of this design and discuss performance forecasts from 10--15-m class telescopes as example platforms.

Items.Authors: Takumi Izawa, Kosuke Aizawa, Ryosuke Akizawa, Scott Cray, Samuel Dietterich, Shaul Hanany, Jürgen Koch, Rex Lam, Asuka Maeda, Tomotake Matsumura, Ryota Takaku
Items.Title: A millimeter-wave transmission measurement system for optical samples cooled to liquid-nitrogen temperature
Items.Abstract: Characterizing optical materials at cryogenic temperatures is crucial for millimeter-wave astronomical receivers. We developed a transmittance measurement system using a liquid-nitrogen cryostat and a vector-network analyzer (VNA). A sample inside the cryostat is cooled to 94 K via a copper strap, while millimeter waves from the VNA pass through a Zotefoam window. A rotatable sample holder allows measurements with and without the sample in a single cryostat run. We measured the transmittance of a 50-mm-diameter, 99.5% purity alumina disk between 140 and 220 GHz at room temperature and 94 K. The refractive index and loss tangent changed from n = 3.083±0.002 and tanδ = (3.6±0.1)×10-4 at room temperature, to n = 3.059±0.002 and tanδ = (0.0±0.1)×10-4 at 94 K.

Items.Authors: Denis Tcherniak, Klavs Rommedahl, Gabriel Cobos Tello, Irfan Kuvvetli, Carol Anne Oxborrow, Desiree Della Monica Ferreira, Jan Raagaard, David Blanquez
Items.Title: A modular and mission agnostic EGSE concept for testing of astronomical space instruments: as applied to NewAthena and Theseus missions
Items.Abstract: We present a standardized, modular Electrical Ground Support Equipment (EGSE) architecture for functional testing of space mission electronics. This system features a reusable controller module and mission-specific modules, all within a 19” rack form factor and powered via Power over Ethernet. Standardized interfaces and REST API control enable rapid adaptation to different devices under test. This approach significantly reduces development time and cost, allowing small engineering teams to efficiently support diverse missions by focusing only on mission-specific requirements.

Items.Authors: Benjamin Boyd, Bryce Warren, Steve Benton, Ajay S. Gill, John Hartley, Bradley Holder, William Jones, Steven Li, C. Barth Netterfield, Emaad Paracha, Susan Redmond, Javier Romualdez, Simon Tartakovsky, Philippe Voyer, Adyn Miles
Items.Title: A modular dynamics simulation framework for the pre-assembly validation of balloon-borne telescope control systems
Items.Abstract: Modern high-altitude astronomical payloads integrate increasingly lightweight structures and complex control systems, making early-stage performance prediction essential for informed design decisions. We present a fully modular, real-time simulation framework developed to test flight software and evaluate payload behaviour before hardware integration, providing a consistent system-level environment for mechanical design, hardware selection, and control-strategy development. The simulator is organized around a configurable architecture in which every payload is specified by bodies, joints, actuators, and sensors, enabling topology changes with little overhead. Development of the framework will continue alongside the Gigapixel Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (GigaBIT) program, validating its flight software through closed-loop dynamics simulations. This approach supports early validation of design concepts, reduces integration risk, and offers a path toward more robust instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Luca Baldini, Ronaldo Bellazzini, Augusto Cattafesta, Paolo Falasca, Juan Sebastian Hincapie Tarquino, Luca Latronico, Alberto Manfreda, Massimo Minuti, Melissa Pesce-Rollins, Alessandro Profeti, Carmelo Sgrò, Stefano Silvestri, Alessandra Taffara
Items.Title: A monolithic gas pixel detector with printed-on-chip multiplication stage for astronomical x-ray polarimetry
Items.Abstract: We present a new gas pixel detector (GPD) concept for astronomical X-ray polarimetry in which the charge-multiplication stage is integrated onto the readout chip by adding two thin, patterned layers above its top metal plane. These, together with the ASIC surface, form a micro-gap-like electron-multiplier structure, now fully monolithic, with a single silicon die acting at the same time as a gas multiplier, charge-collecting anode, and readout electronics. Due to the the sub-micron accuracy of the underlying process and the minimal exposed dielectric, this new class of polarization-sensitive detectors has the potential to improve over the previous generation of GPDs in all key areas, including spurious modulation and time stability.    We have realized and operated several gain structures, both on test substrates and on actual pixelated ASICs, down to 43 micron pitch, and we shall present a full characterization of such devices in terms of gain and energy resolution.

Items.Authors: Alexander Yavorsky, Barak Zackay, Joshua Zak
Items.Title: A phase-gradient based approach to high contrast speckle imaging
Items.Abstract: Phase Gradient Speckle Imaging (PGSI) is a newly proposed method for high-contrast imaging through atmospheric turbulence. Taking inspiration from Speckle Interferometry (SI), PGSI uses the average phase gradient of the Fourier transform of the image to estimate the contrast and position of a faint companion. This makes PGSI an almost drop-in replacement for SI, with the advantage of not requiring prior calibration and superior detection contrast. In this work, we present the theoretical framework of PGSI and test it by observing known binaries from QWSSI at Lowell Discovery Telescope (4.3 m) for sub-minute integrations, achieving 8 magnitudes of contrast at 0.4 arcseconds on a ground-based system without extreme AO.

Items.Authors: Scott Ryan, Thomas Gansheimer, William Goble, Andrew Cline, William Podgorski, Stephanie Melikian
Items.Title: A plan to decommission Hectospec and install Viaspec hardware at the MMT Observatory
Items.Abstract: Following the retirement of the legacy Hectospec and Hectochelle instruments in March 2026, the MMT Observatory is transitioning to the next-generation Viaspec spectrograph. This paper details the mechanical decommissioning of the Hecto platform and the physical installation of Viaspec hardware. To avoid the challenges faced by the original 2002 Hecto installation, the modern framework prioritizes safety by utilizing on-site infrastructure, such as the chamber's 3-ton bridge crane and an exterior scissor lift. This document focuses strictly on physical integration; subsequent on-sky commissioning will be covered in future papers.

Items.Authors: Xuejun Zhang, Frank U. Grupp, Long Xiang, Lingtong Zhang, Helena Lamprecht, Hanna Kellermann
Items.Title: A possible telescope for Theon: feasibility study for a 2-meter aperture silicon carbide optical telescope assembly for the Theon mission concept
Items.Abstract: We present a 2 meter Silicon Carbide (SiC) Optical Telescope Assembly (OTA) basic design, hosting an active secondary mirror. We show compliance for this design with the scientific performance requirements of both flavors of the mission: Theon and Theon*. Furthermore, we show that the OTA complies with the ESA M-class mission boundaries with respect to mass, volume, and mechanical loads. The OTA weight, including the active secondary mirror, is projected to be less than 400 kg.  Simulations show that the SiC OTA is strong enough to be launched (in a vertical configuration) on both, an Ariane-6-2 and a Falcon 9 - Block 5 launch vehicle.   We finally link this analysis to a split test concept presented in another paper of this conference, and how this concept allows a cost and time optimized manufacturing sequence, minimizing schedule-related risks. [Grupp, et al. 2026 this conference]

Items.Authors: Erica Sawczynec, Greg Mace, Cynthia Brooks, Daniel Jaffe, Michelle Grigas, Daniel Wilson
Items.Title: A silicon monolithic cross-dispersed grism for mid-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We report on the process development and manufacturing process for both the high-order entry face and low-order exit face of a silicon monolithic cross-dispersed grism. Additionally, we discuss the preliminary design for a lab prototype medium-resolution (R~10,000) H-band (1.45 – 1.70 um) cross-dispersed grism spectrograph, a proof of concept for future higher-resolution NIR imaging-spectrographs.

Items.Authors: David W. Coutts, Christian Schwab, Tobias Feger, Ali Ghari Zadeh, Ross Zhelem, Sana Syed, Yevgen Kripak, Sameerah Osman, Mark Ferrier, Thomas Walters, Jacob Pember
Items.Title: A simple and effective 3x1 image slicer for coupling into three rectangular fibres
Items.Abstract: Image slicing is an important technique to reconcile large fibre apertures on sky with high resolving power for astronomical spectrometers at medium to large size telescopes. We present a simple and effective image slicer that produces a three by one image slicing configuration, where each slice is coupled into a separate rectangular cross section fibre. A telecentric imaging system is used to produce a magnified image of the fibre output. Two separate mirrors are inserted into opposing sides of the image at approximately 12 degrees to create three separate slices: a straight through central slice, and two singly reflected slices. Each slice is then coupled with its own telecentric imaging system into a rectangular fibre. The whole system is optimised for efficiency.

Items.Authors: Giuseppe Carboni, Andrea Orlati, Sergio Poppi, Carlo Migoni, Matteo Fiorentini, Antonietta A. R. Fara
Items.Title: A unified ZeroMQ-based external access layer for DISCOS: real-time telemetry and remote control for the INAF single-dish radio telescopes
Items.Abstract: Modern radio telescopes require flexible and scalable mechanisms to exchange real-time information and support external control. The three INAF single-dish facilities—SRT, Medicina, and Noto—are operated through the DISCOS control software, based on the ACS framework. While ACS remains a solid foundation, its CORBA-based and pull-oriented interaction model limits modern third-party applications.  We present a new external access layer for DISCOS that provides message-based, non-blocking interfaces for both real-time telemetry streaming and remote control. The architecture employs a lightweight ZeroMQ messaging layer, combining publish/subscribe channels for state-variable distribution with a complementary request/reply gateway for command execution. This design improves scalability, reduces coupling, and enables a more open and future-proof environment for ACS/DISCOS-based facilities.

Items.Authors: David D. S. Hale
Items.Title: A versatile camera interface platform
Items.Abstract: A modular software platform has been developed to support the control of diverse astronomical camera systems from multiple client types. Although every instrument differs in requirements and capabilities, camera systems generally share a core set of operational workflows. In practice, however, camera control software is routinely re-implemented or adapted from earlier systems, resulting in isolated code bases, duplicated functionality, and limited propagation of bug fixes or improvements.     The presented platform addresses these issues by encapsulating shared functionality in a core set of extensible base modules, with hardware- and instrument-specific logic implemented as replaceable extensions. This architecture reduces duplication, centralizes maintenance, and supports scalable integration. Developed for the Caltech Optical Observatories’ Optical/Infrared Instrumentation group, the platform applies to other astronomical instrumentation environments.

Items.Authors: Haeun Chung, Carlos Vargas, Erika Hamden, Hannah Tanquary
Items.Title: A web-based exposure time calculator for the Aspera far-ultraviolet mission
Items.Abstract: We present a web-based exposure time calculator (ETC) developed for the Aspera far-ultraviolet SmallSat mission. Aspera targets extremely faint diffuse O VI emission near 103 to 104 nm, with surface brightness on the order of 1E-18 erg s^-1 cm^-2 arcsec^-2. Accurate S/N modeling is essential for evaluating instrument sensitivity and planning observations. The ETC allows users to compute either the exposure time needed for a desired S/N or the expected S/N for a given integration time. Users can modify spatial binning to explore detectability limits for diffuse emission. The tool implements Aspera’s throughput, detector characteristics, and background estimates in a modular framework and is publicly accessible. This presentation highlights the fundamentals of Aspera ETC framework and its application to other ongoing and future ground and space telescopes.

Items.Authors: Kevin J. Ludwick
Items.Title: Accurately simulating gain and clock-induced charge production in the EMCCD gain register
Items.Abstract: An EMCCD will be used for faint companion detection in the Roman Telescope’s coronograph instrument. As the EM gain increases, the chance of clock-induced charge (CIC) production in the gain register increases, which affects the intended multiplication of charge. I have improved the EMCCD detector simulator used for the Roman Telescope, emccd_detect, so that it accounts for this effect. I demonstrate through maximum likelihood estimation that EMCCD data conform better to the modified probability distribution which accounts for this effect. The use of the modified distribution would in principle improve EMCCD calibration and the accuracy of signal extraction from a frame. I discuss the implementation of this as well as other gain phenomena in emccd_detect and demonstrate the enhanced accuracy of the simulator.

Items.Authors: Matteo Tintori, Daniele Gallieni, Samson Hansraj Sambath Kumar, Roberto Biasi, Mauro Manetti, Gerald Angerer, Vittorio Chiavegato
Items.Title: Adaptive optics for the European Solar Telescope: test results of the adaptive secondary prototype
Items.Abstract: The AdOptica Consortium has developed a novel DM prototype that combines high actuator density with low power dissipation, offering a significant technological step forward for solar AO applications. The prototype has a 200 mm aperture with 90 actuators, featuring a reduced pitch that allows finer spatial correction across the wavefront, essential for managing fast-varying daytime turbulence. While improving scalability and energy efficiency, the prototype inherits all the main characteristics of AdOptica’s baseline technology, such large strokes in tip, tilt, and piston, high static accuracy, and the capability to maintain performance even with several inactive actuators—ensuring system robustness and flexibility. It is particularly suited for daytime turbulence compensation with field stabilisation and for use as a post-focal high-order deformable mirror in multi-conjugate AO systems. The paper presents the test results and the wayforward for the EST adaptive secondary final design.

Items.Authors: William J. Marshall, Megan M. Dubay, Thomas Procter, Hank Corbett, Nicholas M. Law, Alan Vasquez Soto, Lawrence Machia, James A. Dockery, Jonathan Carney, Shannon K. Fitton, Donovan G. Schlekat, Jonah L. Aponte, Alex Bucheli, Thomas Cowart, Collin H. Grimes, Katie M. Fasbender, Amy Sasha Ishiguro, Michael Ronco, Glenn Walters
Items.Title: ADDem: the Argus deep-field demonstrator
Items.Abstract: This presentation describes the development, commissioning, and autonomous operation of the Argus Deep-field Demonstrator (ADDem), a fully-robotic prototype system designed to characterize the upcoming Argus Array’s ability to co-add frames to achieve deep imaging. The system features six co-pointed 20-cm telescopes, each equipped with a 61-MPix Sony IMX455 CMOS detector, imaging a 9.4 square degree field of view at one minute cadence with 1.4”/pixel sampling. The dataset generated by this instrument over the past year of operation has accelerated Argus pipeline development and enabled scientific projects involving bright transient follow-up and high-cadence solar system object observation.

Items.Authors: Noemi Mezzanzanica, Ludovico Bizzarri, Giulia Rancati Cattaneo, Andrea Limonta, Mario Zannoni, Giuseppe Addamo, Mauro Lumia, Oscar A. Peverini
Items.Title: Additive manufacturing ultralight profiled feed horns for space-based sky observations
Items.Abstract: Profiled horn antennas for spaceborne astronomical observations have been prototyped in the 80-170 GHz band using Laser Powder Bed Fusion on Metal (LPBF/M) technology, enabling the fabrication of lightweight, monolithic metallic structures with highly controlled geometries. The LPBF/M process allows the realization of optimized horn profiles capable of delivering low return loss, high beam symmetry, and stable broadband performance essential for cosmic microwave background and sub-millimeter astrophysics missions. The flexibility of additive manufacturing also supports rapid design iteration and scalable array production, making LPBF/M a promising pathway for next-generation high-frequency focal-plane architectures in space astronomy. Towards the assessment of a high TRL, mechanical tests and cryogenic thermal cycling are foreseen.

Items.Authors: Claire Tonsa, Enrico Virgilli, Adriano De Rosa, Carmelo Gargano, Natalia Auricchio, Giovanni De Cesare, Claudio Ferrari, Elena Ferrari, Giuseppe Baldazzi, Riccardo Campana, Ezio Caroli, Marta Civitani, Raffaella Landi, Giuseppe Levi, John B. Stephen, John Rankin, Alfonso Pisapia
Items.Title: Adjustable gamma-ray optics (AGO): active alignment for high-precision Laue lenses
Items.Abstract: Hard X-ray and gamma-ray astronomy above ~70 keV needs focusing optics beyond current capabilities. Laue lenses are the most promising solution, but their development is limited by the challenge of aligning thousands of crystals with arcsecond precision. Adhesive-based mountings introduce angular deviations that exceed requirements. We present “Adjustable Gamma-ray Optics” (AGO), a concept enabling arcsecond alignment and active tuning of each Laue-lens crystal via monolithic flexures actuated by miniature piezo stacks. Each Si(111) crystal is mounted on a tunable lamella, allowing sub-arcsecond Bragg-angle control with minimal area loss. This architecture improves alignment, reduces thermal and mechanical sensitivity, and enables in-flight tuning. A 9-crystal demonstrator with bent crystals, optimized flexures, low-absorption routing, and first alignment strategies validates the approach, paving the way for tunable, high-precision lenses for future missions.

Items.Authors: Wim Pessemier, Gert Raskin, Jacob Pember, Jesus Pérez Padilla, Pieter Vuylsteke, Wim De Meester, Maddalena Reggiani, Christian Schwab, Bart Vandenbussche, Hans Van Winckel
Items.Title: Advanced PLC-based control at the heart of the MARVEL telescope array
Items.Abstract: MARVEL is a high-resolution spectrograph fed by four telescopes, currently being commissioned at the Mercator Observatory on La Palma. At the core of the facility's control architecture is a powerful TwinCAT PLC, which not only manages local devices but also coordinates large parts of the entire facility. We highlight the use of industrial vision for fast tip-tilt guiding, the integration of ASCOM/Alpaca devices, and the implementation of a flexible task sequencer for instrument configuration, all on the PLC platform. The system makes extensive use of a web-based TwinCAT HMI for visualizing these features and for rendering basic 3D views of parts of the facility. Additionally, we describe how an improved model-driven code generation framework has enabled us to efficiently deploy fundamental code changes across the system, to migrate decade-old Mercator code to the most recent PLC platforms, and to drastically reduce HMI CPU load by introducing a Model-View-Controller architecture.

Items.Authors: Matteo Canzari, Fiore De Luise, Mauro Dolci, Gaetano Valentini, Andrea Baldassarre, Simone Benedetti, Filippo Boschi, Amico Di Cianno, Nicola Napoleone, Massimo Quintini, Angelo Valentini
Items.Title: Advancing operations at the Campo Imperatore observing station: integrated modernization of telescopes and infrastructure
Items.Abstract: The Campo Imperatore observing station on the Gran Sasso plateau hosts Italy’s highest professional VIS/NIR facility. Two 1-m telescopes, VIT and WOT, are undergoing a coordinated modernization of hardware, control systems, and software infrastructure. VIT is being upgraded with the new CI2RCE InGaAs NIR imager and enhanced control capabilities, while WOT receives updated electronics. Additional developments include site-wide environmental monitoring, extended control hardware, and an integrated software layer for unified operations. This work presents the current configuration of the station and the ongoing refurbishment efforts, aimed at improving reliability, availability, and full remote operability, and outlines the planned return of VIT to scientific operations with its upgraded instrumentation.
